blocks.text: What Makes a Website Work
A website is a tool that serves a specific purpose for a specific audience. Before you open any builder, you need to know three things: who it's for, what it offers, and what you want visitors to do.
Purpose, Audience, and Action

Every effective website starts with a core purpose — the reason it exists. Then comes the target audience — the specific people it serves. Finally, the primary call to action — the one thing you want visitors to do. Without these three, even a beautiful website won't deliver results.
Define Your Website's Core With AI
You don't need to figure out your website's purpose alone. AI can help you articulate it, but only if you give it enough to work with. Let's see what happens when you try.

Website Structure and Design

You have a website draft with pages and structure — now it's time to give it an identity!

In this lesson, you'll give BrightMinds unique visuals, shape the visitor journey so parents sign up, and add subscription logic so the site can generate revenue.
Visual Identity Makes It Real

A website draft starts to feel like a real product when it has a consistent look and feel. Visual identity includes colors, typography, and personality elements like a mascot. For a children's educational site, a mascot makes the brand instantly recognizable — appealing to kids and trustworthy to parents.

blocks.exampleResponse: Meet Professor Whiskers — a friendly cartoon cat wearing round glasses and a tiny lab coat. Professor Whiskers has big, curious eyes, holds a glowing book, and uses a teal-and-orange color scheme. Simple enough for kids to love, distinctive enough to become a brand icon.
blocks.prompt: Use ChatGPT to generate a mascot concept for BrightMinds.
blocks.template: Design [type] for a children's educational website called BrightMinds. It should look [style] and appeal to [audience].

blocks.text: Meet Professor Whiskers

A text description is a starting point. Let's see the mascot to evaluate it! We will use Midjourney — an AI image generator that creates visuals from text prompts. It's especially strong at stylized, illustrative work — exactly what a mascot needs.

blocks.prompt: Ask Midjourney to create an image of Professor Whiskers based on the concept.
blocks.template: [Subject], cartoon style, round glasses, tiny lab coat, holding a glowing book, [color palette], [style], clean background --ar 1:1 --style raw

blocks.text:
• --ar (aspect ratio) 1:1 sets the aspect ratio to a square — ideal for mascots and logos that need to work across different placements.
  • --style raw tells Midjourney to follow your prompt more literally instead of adding its own artistic interpretation. For a brand mascot that needs to look consistent and controllable, these two parameters keep the output clean and usable.
blocks.title: Midjourney Parameters

The Visitor Journey
A visitor journey is the path someone takes from arriving on your site to completing the action you want. Every page, section, and button should move them one step closer.

In Lesson 1, you've already navigated the user's journey towards a clear action within the main page. You also created an additional page on your website. Let's now dive deeper into the whole website visitor's journey design.
Map It Before You Build It
Most websites lose visitors because the journey has gaps — unclear next steps, missing information, or dead ends. AI can help you spot these gaps before you redesign anything.

blocks.exampleResponse:
1. Homepage hero → clicks "How It Works"
  2. “How it Works" → understands the system and the value, goes to the subject catalogue
  3. Subject catalog → chooses a lesson
  4. Free sample content→ completes it, sees "Want more?" prompt
  5. Pricing page → compares Free vs. Premium
  6. Checkout → starts free trial
Each transition has one clear action.

blocks.text: Navigation Should Match the Journey

You've mapped the path — now the site's navigation needs to support it. Right now, your menu probably lists every page equally. But not every page deserves top-level navigation. You should move the pages that distract from the main journey to the footer or remove them entirely.

blocks.text: Great!
The site now guides visitors from curiosity to action without detours. Let's add the feature that makes this business work.
Gated Content and Subscriptions

BrightMinds offers educational lessons — some free, some behind a subscription. This is called gated content: certain pages or features are only available to paying users. The free content proves the product is worth it. The gated content gives people a reason to pay.
Set Up Gated Content in Lovable

Adding a subscription model starts with telling Lovable which content is free and which is paid. In your chat panel, describe the split clearly: "Make the first lesson in each subject free. Gate quizzes, progress tracking, and advanced lessons behind a Premium subscription."
Free and Premium Labels

Lovable will add Free and Premium badges to your lesson cards in the catalog. Free lessons are open to any visitor. Premium lessons are visually marked so parents know what's included in each tier before they click.
Check the Flow

Preview the site and click through as a parent would. Open a free lesson — it should load without any barriers. Then click a Premium lesson — the modal should appear immediately with a clear path to sign up. If anything feels off, describe the issue in the chat panel, and Lovable will adjust it.

• Visual identity — colors, mascot, typography — makes a website feel like a real product, not a draft.
  • The visitor journey is the path from landing to action — every page and button should move users closer to the goal.
  • Navigation should support the journey, not clutter it — remove pages that create detours.
  • Gated content works best when the free tier proves the product's value and the paid tier deepens the experience.

blocks.text: Website Structure and Design

You have a website draft with pages and structure — now it's time to give it an identity!

In this lesson, you'll give BrightMinds unique visuals, shape the visitor journey so parents sign up, and add subscription logic so the site can generate revenue.
Visual Identity Makes It Real

A website draft starts to feel like a real product when it has a consistent look and feel. Visual identity includes colors, typography, and personality elements like a mascot. For a children's educational site, a mascot makes the brand instantly recognizable — appealing to kids and trustworthy to parents.

blocks.exampleResponse: Meet Professor Whiskers — a friendly cartoon cat wearing round glasses and a tiny lab coat. Professor Whiskers has big, curious eyes, holds a glowing book, and uses a teal-and-orange color scheme. Simple enough for kids to love, distinctive enough to become a brand icon.

blocks.text: Meet Professor Whiskers

A text description is a starting point. Let's see the mascot to evaluate it! We will use Midjourney — an AI image generator that creates visuals from text prompts. It's especially strong at stylized, illustrative work — exactly what a mascot needs.

blocks.prompt: Ask Midjourney to create an image of Professor Whiskers based on the concept.
blocks.template: [Subject], cartoon style, round glasses, tiny lab coat, holding a glowing book, [color palette], [style], clean background --ar 1:1 --style raw

  • --style raw tells Midjourney to follow your prompt more literally instead of adding its own artistic interpretation. For a brand mascot that needs to look consistent and controllable, these two parameters keep the output clean and usable.

The Visitor Journey
A visitor journey is the path someone takes from arriving on your site to completing the action you want. Every page, section, and button should move them one step closer.

In Lesson 1, you've already navigated the user's journey towards a clear action within the main page. You also created an additional page on your website. Let's now dive deeper into the whole website visitor's journey design.
Map It Before You Build It
Most websites lose visitors because the journey has gaps — unclear next steps, missing information, or dead ends. AI can help you spot these gaps before you redesign anything.

Each transition has one clear action.

Build a Simple No-Code App

A parent discovers your website, browses a few lessons, and subscribes. Great! They now need BrightMinds to be on their phone: quick to open, easy to pick up where they left off, built around a daily routine.

In this lesson, you're about to build your no-code app. Let's get started!
Define the App's Purpose

Before you build anything, get specific about what the app does. An app isn't a smaller version of your website — it's a focused tool for a specific workflow. 

For BrightMinds, that workflow is: a child logs in, picks a lesson, completes it, and tracks their progress.

blocks.exampleResponse: Core screens: Home dashboard, Subject browser, Lesson player, Progress tracker, Profile Key actions: pick a lesson, complete activities, take quizzes, earn badges Data to track: completed lessons, quiz scores, badges earned, time spent per subject

Your First Prompt in Bolt.new
Just like with Lovable, specificity drives quality. Your first prompt should include what the app does, who it's for, which screens to build, and the overall style.

Upload two reference files into Bolt.new's chat: a screenshot of your BrightMinds website from Lovable and the Professor Whiskers mascot image from Midjourney. Bolt.new will use them as visual references to match the app's style to your existing brand. Let's generate the first app draft.

blocks.text: How Bolt.new Works

The Bolt.new interface will look familiar. On the left, the chat panel where you type prompts and follow-ups. On the right, a live preview of your app that updates as the AI builds. Every change you request happens through conversation — same workflow as Lovable.
Navigating Your App

Bolt.new organizes your app with a bottom tab bar — the row of icons at the bottom of the screen. Each tab links to a main screen. This is standard for mobile-style apps: familiar to anyone who's used a phone. You can rename tabs, reorder them, or add new ones through follow-up prompts.
The Key Difference

Unlike Lovable, Bolt.new generates a full-stack app — meaning it handles both what the user sees (the interface) and the logic behind it (data storage, user accounts, tracking). When you ask it to track quiz scores, it builds the system that stores and retrieves the data.
Refining the App
You have a working app draft with five screens and navigation. Let's refine the most important screen first — the one users see every time they open the app.
The Home Dashboard

The dashboard is where engagement lives. A child opening the app should immediately see what to do next. The best dashboards answer three questions: What did I do last? What should I do next? How am I doing overall?

blocks.prompt: Write a follow-up prompt to improve the BrightMinds home dashboard.
blocks.template: Redesign the BrightMinds home dashboard to show [element] at the top, a recommended next lesson in the middle, and a progress summary with badges at the bottom. Use [tone] language like "Ready for your next adventure?"

feedbackCorrect.text: A wall of 40 lessons gives a child no direction. A strong dashboard is curated — it highlights what's relevant right now: the last lesson, the next recommendation, and a progress snapshot. Less choice, more action.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Alphabetical lists are organized, but organization isn't the same as guidance. A 7-year-old opening the app doesn't want to browse — they want to know what to do next. The dashboard's job is to answer that question instantly.

blocks.text: Build the Lesson Player

The lesson player is where learning happens. It needs to feel different from a website article. App lessons should be interactive: short content sections, tappable elements, a quiz at the end, and clear feedback on every answer.

blocks.prompt: Prompt Bolt.new to build an interactive lesson experience.
blocks.template: Build the BrightMinds lesson player [format]: a short [content], then an interactive activity, then [assessment]. Show [feedback] after each answer when the lesson is done.

blocks.text: None of This Saves Without Login

You've built a dashboard and a lesson player. But if a child closes the app and reopens it, their progress is gone. The app needs user accounts to store data per user. Bolt.new handles authentication out of the box — you just need to ask for it.

blocks.prompt: Prompt Bolt.new to add login and account creation to BrightMinds.
blocks.template: Add user authentication to BrightMinds. Let parents [action]. After login, the app should  show the child's dashboard and load [data]. Add [element] to the profile screen.

blocks.text: Test Before You Share

Your app has screens, data, and user accounts. Before going further, you need to test it the way a real user would. Bolt.new lets you preview the app in your browser — and you can open the preview link on your phone to see how it feels on a mobile screen.
How to Test Your App
Click the preview link in the top right corner of Bolt.new's editor. This opens your app in a new browser tab. To test on mobile, copy the preview URL and open it on your phone.

Walk through the full flow: create an account, browse subjects, start a lesson, complete a quiz, and check if progress saves correctly. If anything breaks, describe the issue in Bolt.new's chat panel — be specific about what happened and what you expected.
Connect the Website to the App

Many products work across both a website and an app. BrightMinds is no different. The point is to make both options visible and easy to access. Right now, a parent who signs up on the website has no way to find the app.

blocks.prompt: Prompt Lovable to add an app download or access section to the BrightMinds website.
blocks.template: Add [section] to the website. Include [element] with the text "Start Learning in the App" and [content] why the app experience is usable for daily learning.

blocks.text: Great Work!
BrightMinds now lives in two places — a website and an app — delivering the daily learning experience. Both are connected, branded consistently, and built entirely from natural language prompts.

• Define screens, actions, and data before you start building an app.
  • Upload your references in Bolt.new to keep the brand consistent.
  • The home dashboard should answer "What do I do next?", not show everything at once.
  • Connect your website and app, so subscribers know where to go after signing up.

Add AI Features and Automation

You have two products in your portfolio — BrightMinds, an educational platform, and FitBase, a booking app. Before you launch either one, there's a question worth asking: where could these products be smarter? In this lesson, you'll add AI features and automations that make both products stronger, more useful, and harder to compete with.

Let's get started!
AI as a Product Extension

Adding AI to a product is about finding the moments where the product could respond, assist, or act — and currently doesn't. A child stuck on a lesson with no one to ask. A gym member who knows what class they want but has to scroll through the whole schedule to find it. AI fills those gaps.
Different Products, Different AI

Different products need different AI features. An educational platform benefits from features that assist learning. A booking app benefits from features that reduce friction. Before you build anything, ask: what's the core action, and where does the user get stuck or slow down?
AI for BrightMinds — A Tutor Chatbot

Your educational platform teaches kids about science and the humanities. But a lesson doesn't cover everything. An AI tutor chatbot gives kids a place to ask follow-up questions and get age-appropriate answers, right inside the lesson.

The tutor chatbot helps kids go deeper into a lesson they've already found. But what about finding the right lesson in the first place? Right now, a child has to browse through categories manually. That's fine for adults, but challenging for a 7-year-old.
AI for BrightMinds — Smart Search
A smart search feature lets them type (or even ask) what they want to learn — "I want to learn about dinosaurs" — and the AI finds the right lesson, even if the child doesn't use the exact title.

The tutor chatbot and smart search solve different problems: one helps kids learn deeper, the other helps them find content faster. But both follow the same rule: they respond to what the user is doing at the moment. That's the test for any AI feature. Let's apply it to FitBase.
Let's Work on FitBase
FitBase has different problems to solve. The studio owner currently sends booking confirmations by hand, and every member sees the same schedule regardless of what they book. Let's fix it!
AI for FitBase — A Booking Assistant

FitBase members know what they want — "yoga tomorrow morning" — but the app makes them scroll through a full schedule to find it. An AI booking assistant lets members type or tap a quick request and get matched to the right class instantly. It turns a browse-and-search task into a single sentence.

blocks.text: Great job!
You've just implemented pro AI features into your products to make them more user-friendly. But every product has many background tasks that require automation. Let's handle them!
From AI to Automation

AI features respond to user behavior in real time. Automations handle the tasks that happen in the background — sending confirmations, following up after no-shows, notifying members when a spot opens up.
Meet Zapier

Zapier connects your apps to other tools — like email, SMS, or calendar — through simple "if this, then that" rules called Zaps. When something happens in your app, Zapier triggers an action elsewhere (e.g., sending a confirmation email). No code needed.
The bridge between your app and Zapier is a webhook — a URL that Zapier generates, and your app sends data to whenever something happens.

That's how the setup works: you create a Zap in Zapier and choose "Webhooks by Zapier" as the trigger. Select "Catch Hook" — this tells Zapier to listen for incoming data. Zapier generates a unique webhook URL. Copy it.

Then go to Bolt.new and prompt, "When a new booking is created, send the booking details (class name, date, time, member email) to this webhook URL:" and paste the URL. This tells your app to push data to Zapier every time a booking happens.
Now add an Action — what happens after the trigger fires. Choose Gmail (or Email by Zapier if you don't want to connect a Gmail account). Select "Send Email" as the action event.
Click "Test action" to send a real test email. Check your inbox. If it looks right, publish the Zap — it's now live and will send a confirmation email for every new FitBase booking automatically.
Automations Live
Your product now has automations running in the background. But AI and automation need rules — especially when they touch real users.

Monetize and Launch the Product

Both BrightMinds and FitBase have AI features and automations. But neither product is making money yet. 

In this lesson, you'll connect both products to real revenue — set up payments, prepare for launch, and get them in front of actual users.
Pricing Client Work
Building websites and apps with no-code tools is a real, sellable skill. There's no single right way to charge. But the wrong way is to guess. Your pricing should reflect:

• Scope: How much are you building?
  • Value: What is it worth to the client's business?
  • Ongoing relationship: Will they need updates after launch?
Pricing Models
There are three models:

• One-time project fee: You build it, hand it off, done. Works when the scope is clear, and the client won't need regular changes.
  • Monthly retainer: You maintain and update the product on an ongoing basis. Works when the product needs frequent adjustments.
  • Hybrid: A project fee to build, plus a smaller monthly retainer for maintenance. This is the most common model for app and website work.

feedbackCorrect.text: Ongoing updates mean ongoing work. A one-time fee leaves you doing free labor or forces awkward renegotiations every time they need a change. A hybrid model — say, $2000 to build plus $300/month for maintenance — sets clear expectations and gives you predictable income.

feedbackIncorrect.text: If the client needs regular updates, a one-time fee creates a lose-lose. Either you do unpaid work to keep them happy, or you say no, and they're stuck with a stale app. A retainer turns this into a sustainable relationship where both sides know what to expect.

blocks.text: Prepare for Launch

You've priced the work and written the proposal. Now both products — BrightMinds and FitBase — need to go from builder drafts to real, public-facing products. That starts with giving them a proper address on the internet.
Custom Domains

A domain is your product's address on the internet — what people type into their browser to find you. Right now, your products live on builder subdomains (brightminds.lovable.app or fitbase.bolt.new.) That works for testing, but not for launch.

A custom domain (brightminds.com, fitbasestudio.com) makes the product look professional and trustworthy. You purchase domains through providers like Namecheap, Google Domains, or Cloudflare — search for the name you want, check if it's available, and buy it for around $10-$15 per year.
Connect a Domain in Lovable

In your Lovable project, go to Publish and click "Add Custom Domain" (paid feature). Enter the domain you purchased, and Lovable gives you the option to add to your domain provider. This points your domain to Lovable's servers.
Hosting

Hosting is where your product's files live on the internet. The good news: both Lovable and Bolt.new handle hosting for you. When you publish your project, your product is hosted automatically. For most projects, this built-in hosting is enough. If a client needs advanced hosting (custom server, specific region), you can export the code from either builder and host it on platforms like Netlify or Vercel.
SEO Basics

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) helps your product appear in Google results. Parents searching "fun science lessons for kids" will find BrightMinds. Setting up SEO is a skill that adds value to every project you build.
What Search Engines Need
Every page needs two things to rank: a title tag (the clickable headline in search results) and a meta description (the short text underneath).
Good title tags are specific, include keywords, and stay under 60 characters. Meta descriptions should be under 160 characters and describe the page's value.

blocks.text: Monetize and Launch the Product

Both BrightMinds and FitBase have AI features and automations. But neither product is making money yet. 

In this lesson, you'll connect both products to real revenue — set up payments, prepare for launch, and get them in front of actual users.
Pricing Client Work
Building websites and apps with no-code tools is a real, sellable skill. There's no single right way to charge. But the wrong way is to guess. Your pricing should reflect:

• Scope: How much are you building?
  • Value: What is it worth to the client's business?
  • Ongoing relationship: Will they need updates after launch?
Pricing Models
There are three models:

• One-time project fee: You build it, hand it off, done. Works when the scope is clear, and the client won't need regular changes.
  • Monthly retainer: You maintain and update the product on an ongoing basis. Works when the product needs frequent adjustments.
  • Hybrid: A project fee to build, plus a smaller monthly retainer for maintenance. This is the most common model for app and website work.

feedbackCorrect.text: Ongoing updates mean ongoing work. A one-time fee leaves you doing free labor or forces awkward renegotiations every time they need a change. A hybrid model — say, $2000 to build plus $300/month for maintenance — sets clear expectations and gives you predictable income.

feedbackIncorrect.text: If the client needs regular updates, a one-time fee creates a lose-lose. Either you do unpaid work to keep them happy, or you say no, and they're stuck with a stale app. A retainer turns this into a sustainable relationship where both sides know what to expect.

blocks.text: Prepare for Launch

You've priced the work and written the proposal. Now both products — BrightMinds and FitBase — need to go from builder drafts to real, public-facing products. That starts with giving them a proper address on the internet.
Custom Domains

A domain is your product's address on the internet — what people type into their browser to find you. Right now, your products live on builder subdomains (brightminds.lovable.app or fitbase.bolt.new.) That works for testing, but not for launch.

A custom domain (brightminds.com, fitbasestudio.com) makes the product look professional and trustworthy. You purchase domains through providers like Namecheap, Google Domains, or Cloudflare — search for the name you want, check if it's available, and buy it for around $10-$15 per year.
Connect a Domain in Lovable

In your Lovable project, go to Publish and click "Add Custom Domain" (paid feature). Enter the domain you purchased, and Lovable gives you the option to add to your domain provider. This points your domain to Lovable's servers.
Hosting

Hosting is where your product's files live on the internet. The good news: both Lovable and Bolt.new handle hosting for you. When you publish your project, your product is hosted automatically. For most projects, this built-in hosting is enough. If a client needs advanced hosting (custom server, specific region), you can export the code from either builder and host it on platforms like Netlify or Vercel.
SEO Basics

SEO (Search Engine Optimization) helps your product appear in Google results. Parents searching "fun science lessons for kids" will find BrightMinds. Setting up SEO is a skill that adds value to every project you build.
What Search Engines Need
Every page needs two things to rank: a title tag (the clickable headline in search results) and a meta description (the short text underneath).
Good title tags are specific, include keywords, and stay under 60 characters. Meta descriptions should be under 160 characters and describe the page's value.

Improve Performance

Your product is now live. But "live" doesn't mean "done." Some users might sign up and never come back. Others might start the checkout and abandon it.

In this final lesson, you'll learn to read what your users are telling you through their behavior and make the changes that improve results. Let's finish strong!
What "Performance" Actually Means
Performance indicates whether the product achieves its goal. Every product has a small set of numbers that tell you if it's working. Those are your metrics.
For different products, you will track different metrics.

• For BrightMinds: are parents subscribing, are kids completing lessons, and are families staying month after month?
  • For FitBase: are members booking classes, showing up, and renewing?
Pick the Right Metrics

The most common mistake is tracking everything. Page views, button clicks, scroll depth — most of it is noise. What you need are actionable metrics: numbers that, if they change, tell you exactly what to fix. Each product has different ones.

correctTokens: why it matters and what a change signals
blocks.exampleResponse:
1. Booking rate: What percentage of app opens result in a class booking? A drop signals friction in the booking flow or irrelevant class options.
  2. Class fill rate: Are classes reaching capacity or running half-empty? Low fill rates mean scheduling or pricing needs adjustment.
  3. No-show rate: How many booked members don't attend? A high rate indicates weak reminders or no cancellation incentive.
  4. Repeat booking rate: Are members booking again within 7 days? A decline signals engagement problems — members aren't forming a habit.

blocks.text: Set Up Tracking

You can't improve what you can't measure. Lovable already includes its own analytics. You can use Google Analytics if you want extra tracking and are adding the Google tag to the project yourself. Google Analytics is a free tool that tracks how users behave on your website or app: which pages they visit, where they drop off, and what actions they take. Let's add it to your product.
Create a Google Analytics property for your website and open your web data stream to find the measurement ID (the code that starts with G-).

To connect Analytics to your site, you either enter that ID into a builder that supports Google Analytics directly or add the full Google tag code to your site. Once the tag is installed, Google Analytics can start collecting visitor data.
In Bolt.new, you can add Google Analytics by inserting the Google tag code into your site — either manually in Code view or by asking Bolt.new in the chat to add it for you.
Find the Bottleneck

Metrics tell you the product is underperforming. Bottleneck analysis tells you where. A bottleneck is the single point in your user flow where the most people drop off. Fix that one point, and everything downstream improves.
Let's Look at FitBase

The FitBase studio owner tells you, "People book classes but don't show up. My no-show rate is around 30%." This is a retention problem. And it costs the studio real money because every empty spot could have gone to another member.

blocks.exampleResponse:
Likely causes: — Members book impulsively and forget. — There's no penalty for missing a class. — Reminders aren't sent close enough to class time. Suggested fixes:
  1. Send a push notification hours before the class with a "Confirm or Cancel" button.
  2. Add a soft penalty: after 3 no-shows in a month, the member loses priority booking for a week.
  3. Show a "Your class is in 2 hours" card on the home screen when the app is opened on class day.

blocks.text: The Iteration Mindset

Products that stay the same after launch slowly die. Products need to iterate based on real data to get better every week.

You don't need to rebuild everything at once. Measure, find the weak point, and make one targeted change at a time.

blocks.title: Product Improvement Cycle

blocks.text:
• Track actionable metrics, not everything: Focus on numbers that tell you exactly what to fix, like no-show rates — not general stats like page views.
  • Find the bottleneck first: The single biggest drop-off point in your flow is where improvement has the most impact.
  • Use AI to analyze problems and suggest fixes: Upload your data into ChatGPT to identify causes and prioritize solutions.
  • Improvement is a loop, not a one-time event: Measure, identify, fix, measure again — products that stop iterating stop growing.
